name: Jamal Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. We don't sell or campaign for anything. Your answers are confidential. What is an ordinary workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I get to the Mill Court site before seven and check the timber stack for bent boards. I am fifty-eight, but I'm the new fellow in carpentry after a long stretch driving delivery vans; I left school early and have to ask when a joint is new to me. I use an AI assistant on my phone every day to make a cutting list or explain a drawing, then check the numbers against the plan. My partner Farah works at a bakery, and our grown sons live on their own. I enjoy fitting skirting cleanly, though the heavy boards are harder than they were ten years ago.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the phone tool is already handy for sorting a cutting list, and a plateau would leave room to use it without turning every job upside down. A machine cannot nail a board that has warped since delivery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm happy to keep earning normal site wages, but I know I'm a beginner among men half my age. Farah and I have about five months of expenses tucked away, and bakery hours can jump around in winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep using the phone assistant for lists and check each cut against the drawing. In the first year I'll take every paid skirting shift I can and keep our regular transfer into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel fairly easy about the technology, because I have already made it useful. The site calendar still matters; a missing week's work would be felt at home even with our cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where has the phone assistant made a mistake?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It once counted the same doorway twice from a rough sketch, so I walked the room and crossed out the extra trim. I won't let a phone decide how much timber I cut without looking myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do your sons think of your late start in carpentry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My sons laugh that their old dad studies joints over dinner, but they can see I like the work. I don't want them paying our rent just because I'm learning slowly.

say: I'd say the **phone assistant** helps with cutting lists while site work continues.
I'd remind the crew **warped timber** still needs a worker's eye.
think: I'm a **junior carpenter** despite my age and normal site pay.
Our **five-month cushion** must also cover Farah's uneven bakery hours.
do: Use the **phone assistant** for lists and verify each cut.
Take paid **skirting shifts** and keep the usual savings transfer.
feel: Fairly **easy** about the tool, with the site calendar still in mind.
S0.quote: I won't let a phone decide how much timber I cut without looking myself.
fieldNote: Jamal's daily AI use is grounded in a real **double-counting error** and a habit of checking the room.
A **five-month reserve** gives some room, but junior status and Farah's variable bakery hours keep income unsettled.

steps.text: Use the phone assistant for checked cutting lists
Keep taking paid skirting shifts at Mill Court

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the software may do buying and planning faster, so we should learn it before it starts making our orders. I would still ask who checks a timber order when the site drawing changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the firm's office may shrink and the Mill Court crew could be kept waiting for its next job. I can learn the new system quickly, but being a late-entry junior means I may be first off if the pipeline slows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask supervisor Dev to let me trial the new ordering screen with the buyer and take photos of any errors we catch. During the first year I'll keep taking site shifts, and if two weeks disappear from the board I'll phone three local builders about openings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel keyed up but also interested; a good tool could save a lot of wasted trips. Farah's bakery hours and my place on the roster stop me from treating this as a game.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to learn first on the ordering screen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn how to update quantities when a drawing changes, because that is where the wrong boards turn up. The buyer has already shown me how one changed door size affects the whole list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why call builders after two missing weeks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two empty weeks would use a chunk of savings and tell me the pipeline is weak. I know a man at each of those builders from van deliveries, so I'd ask for actual paid work.

say: I'd urge the crew to learn **new ordering** before mistakes reach the site.
I'd ask who checks quantities after a **drawing change**.
think: A smaller office could create **site gaps** between contracts.
My **late-entry junior** position makes a slow roster personally risky.
do: Trial the **ordering screen** with the buyer and record errors.
Keep taking **site shifts** while work remains.
Phone **three builders** after two missing workweeks.
feel: **Interested and keyed up**, with the household income risk close by.
S1.quote: Farah's bakery hours and my place on the roster stop me from treating this as a game.
fieldNote: Jamal responds to disruption by testing the **ordering system** against changed drawings rather than refusing it.
His threshold for a job search is **two missing weeks**, a concrete limit shaped by savings and bakery hours.

steps.text: Trial the AI ordering screen with the site buyer
Phone three local builders after two missing weeks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the crew should get in front of the 2028 thinking system by learning its site tools now. Robots that can fit timber in 2031 are the bigger change for our hands, and we ought to hear the firm's plan early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty when estimates and drawings can be done by AI, so site jobs may change before a robot lifts a board. At sixty-three I could lose the fitting hours themselves, and five months of expenses won't bridge an unknown stretch of unemployment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting this winter I'll test the AI drawing checker with Dev and put extra money aside from full weeks. In 2029 I'll take the available paid carpentry shifts and apply for paid building-maintenance posts if the work board thins; by 2031 I'd also ask the trade association about any funded repair apprenticeship, though I would enrol only if the placement pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel a jolt at how fast the dates come, then I start writing things down. I have enough energy to try a new route, but I cannot bet Farah's rent money on a course with no wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the drawing checker need to prove?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It must catch a missing measurement before timber is ordered, and Dev needs to see the same result I do. One clever answer on my phone is not proof for a full site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your sons help if the work went?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They would offer, but both have young households and their own costs. I'd rather accept a paid placement than ask them to cover our bills.

say: I'd say we should learn **site AI** before the 2028 change.
I'd ask for the firm's **robot plan** before 2031 fitting work changes.
think: At **sixty**, drawings and estimates could alter contracts before robots arrive.
At **sixty-three**, lost fitting hours could outlast our five-month reserve.
do: Test the **drawing checker** with Dev and save extra from full weeks.
Keep taking **paid shifts** in 2029 and apply for maintenance openings.
Ask about a **paid repair apprenticeship** if hands-on work falls.
feel: A sharp **jolt**, followed by practical curiosity and household caution.
S2.quote: I cannot bet Farah's rent money on a course with no wage.
fieldNote: He distinguishes immediate changes to drawings from the later threat to fitting, then puts each on a **dated work plan**.
His willingness to retrain is conditional on a **funded paid placement**, consistent with his five-month reserve.

steps.text: Test the AI drawing checker with Dev
Save extra from full paid weeks
Apply for paid building-maintenance posts if the work board thins
Enrol in a repair apprenticeship only if the placement pays

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the site team five years is enough to learn a tool properly and build a stronger record of completed rooms. I wouldn't tell anyone that a good record alone will beat the robots of 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At sixty-three, AI could do the planning that feeds our work, and at sixty-six the robot could fit skirting as well as a person. I might choose retirement then, but I have no reliable pension figure to wave around today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask Dev to let me keep a log of finished rooms and the AI checks I run, then save a little more after each full month. In 2032 I'd take paid carpentry work while it exists and look at maintenance vacancies with real wage figures; if the hours disappear, I'd apply, not merely talk about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel more organised with five years, though I still dislike the idea of being junior when robots arrive. There is time to show that I can learn, not a guarantee that someone will hire me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep a log of finished rooms?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I arrived late to the trade, so a future foreman cannot judge me by twenty years of jobs. Photos and signed room lists could show what I actually completed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What figure would make retirement possible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Farah and I would total our bills and savings and find out what income really continues after work. Until then, a retirement date is a hope, not a budget.

say: I'd say five years allows **proper tool learning** and a record of completed rooms.
I'd warn that a good **work record** cannot guarantee 2034 site hours.
think: At **sixty-three**, thinking AI may change the planning that feeds our crew.
At **sixty-six**, retirement remains uncertain without actual income figures.
do: Record **finished rooms** and AI checks with Dev.
Save more after **full months** and take paid work in 2032.
Apply to **maintenance vacancies** if carpentry hours vanish.
feel: More **organised**, while junior status remains a real weakness.
S3.quote: Until then, a retirement date is a hope, not a budget.
fieldNote: Jamal's **five-year plan** uses photographs and signed work lists to compensate for entering carpentry late.
He will apply for maintenance only if site hours vanish and keeps retirement conditional on **actual household figures**.

steps.text: Keep a signed log of finished rooms and AI checks
Save extra after full paid months
Apply to paid maintenance vacancies if site hours vanish

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years gives a worker time to earn, learn and see what tools actually stick. By 2039 there may be robots on sites, but I'd be surprised if I were still carrying heavy boards at seventy-one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At sixty-eight when the thinking system arrives, I may still want paid lighter repair work; at seventy-one, robots could take that too. Farah and I can plan toward stopping, but our present savings and uncertain bakery hours don't prove we can afford it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep taking site work, use AI for checked cutting lists, and build our savings while my body allows full weeks. In 2037 I'd look for paid small repair jobs if we still need income, and Farah and I would review our real income before deciding whether I can step off the site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel roomy about the technology date, even a bit hopeful about having tools for another decade. I still keep an eye on winter bakery hours and my back, which need attention now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy a robot for a small repair business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I wouldn't tie our savings to a machine I have never seen earn its keep. I'd rather take a real paid repair call than own a costly bit of hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a young worker starting now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my younger mate to learn both the trade and the checking tools while he is being paid. A phone answer is useful, but a bad cut still wastes a board.

say: I'd say a **decade** gives workers time to earn and learn.
I'd doubt I will carry **heavy boards** at seventy-one.
think: At **sixty-eight**, I may still need paid lighter repairs.
At **seventy-one**, robots could take those repairs before we can afford to stop.
do: Keep taking **site work** and using checked AI cutting lists.
Build **savings** from full weeks and seek paid repairs in 2037.
Review **real income** with Farah before leaving work.
feel: **Roomy and hopeful** about the dates, while current work and bakery hours remain uncertain.
S4.quote: A phone answer is useful, but a bad cut still wastes a board.
fieldNote: The **long horizon** brings hope, but he continues to calculate a need for paid work after thinking AI arrives.
He rejects buying a robot with **household savings** and keeps retirement tied to verified income, not age alone.

steps.text: Keep taking paid site work while physically able
Use AI for checked cutting lists on current jobs
Build savings from full paid weeks

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture worries me most, since I would have only three years from thinking AI to site robots and I'm still a new carpenter. A paid route into repairs, honest work board dates and time to test the drawing tools with Dev would help me earn while I learn.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether workers get to see the mistake log when an AI order goes wrong. A tool can improve, but the person cutting the boards needs to know what failed yesterday.

headlineQuote: A machine cannot nail a board that has warped since delivery.
portrait: Jamal is a **fifty-eight-year-old junior** carpenter after years of delivery driving.
He uses an **AI phone assistant daily**, checking its lists against plans and the room.
His five-month reserve supports a household with **variable bakery hours**.
He pursues **paid learning** and real openings while refusing to assume retirement or buy an unproven robot.
biggestWorry: The **2028 path** leaves only three years before robots may take his hands-on fitting work.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **paid repair training**, clear work board dates and supervised time to test drawing tools.
